clue.text: The world of Powell finds approbation.

definitions.meaning: Anthony Powell's novel in A Dance to the Music of Time is titled with this word before 'World'
approval, a willing taking-on of something

explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Powell's novel sequence A Dance to the Music of Time includes The Acceptance World, so 'The world of Powell' points to the word that precedes 'World' in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Approbation is approval, and agreeing to receive something favourably is the same idea, a synonym.

clue.text: Wife of Alcinous turned into a tree.

indicators.note: turned into signals that the letters of the two words are rearranged to form something new

explanation.surface: A mythical queen, like Daphne, is transformed into a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned into' suggests an Ovid-style metamorphosis, but it is the anagram signal working on A TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Odyssey the queen of the Phaeacians, consort of King Alcinous, bears this name.

clue.text: Conceited poet, ex-President.

definitions.meaning: John ... was a seventeenth-century Metaphysical poet, famous for elaborate conceits
Grover ... served twice as President of the United States

explanation.walkthrough: 'Conceited' is not 'vain' but 'given to conceits', the far-fetched metaphors of the Metaphysical school.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname is shared by the royalist Metaphysical poet John and the American leader Grover, both famous bearers.

clue.text: Haunting verses by Carroll.

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's long comic poem about a ghost who haunts a house gives its title to his collection, a word for a shifting dreamlike show of images

explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's comic poem about a ghost, which titles his 1869 collection, is named with a word for a sequence of ghostly projected images.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a shifting series of dreamlike or ghostly images, apt for a poem about a haunting spectre.

clue.text: Joseph answer'd wrongly!

indicators.note: wrongly tells us the letters of the word answer'd are set down in a mistaken order

explanation.surface: Someone named Joseph has replied incorrectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'answer'd' looks like a verb about Joseph, but its seven letters, rearranged as 'wrongly' directs, give the surname of Fielding's hero.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Fielding's novel Joseph Andrews names its hero, so the forename stands for his surname by association.

clue.text: Unromantic girl in Tully's arms briefly.

indicators.note: being in someone's arms means being embraced, so one piece is held inside another
briefly asks for the name to be cut short, to its standard scholarly abbreviation

parts.note: Tully is the old English name for Marcus Tullius Cicero, abbreviated Cic. in references
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An unsentimental young woman is embraced for a moment by the Roman orator.
explanation.walkthrough: Tully is the traditional English name for Cicero; 'briefly' cuts CICERO to CIC, whose 'arms' hold LASS.
explanation.definitionFit: In criticism the classical style is set against the romantic, so restrained and unromantic describes it, an antonym pairing.

clue.text: Great work left half-finished by Epicurus.

indicators.note: a name left only half-finished keeps just its first four of eight letters

explanation.surface: A philosopher abandons his magnum opus midway.
explanation.walkthrough: Epicurus has eight letters; leaving it 'half-finished' keeps the first four.
explanation.definitionFit: A grand heroic poem or any monumental piece of art is a great work.

clue.text: He gave his name to a kind of flat love!

definitions.text: He gave his name to a kind of flat love!

parts.note: plat is an old word for flat, as in a plat or plot of level ground
love is zero in tennis, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone is credited with naming a dull, passionless sort of romance.
explanation.walkthrough: Platonic love is love without physical passion, so 'flat' love; PLAT (an old word for flat) plus O (love, zero in tennis) gives the Greek philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Platonic love, affection without desire, takes its name from the Athenian philosopher who wrote the Symposium.

clue.text: Frederick Clegg, lepidopterist, killer.

parts.note: John Fowles's first novel is narrated by a butterfly-catching clerk who kidnaps a young woman, and its title is what he does to butterflies and to her

explanation.walkthrough: Frederick Clegg is the butterfly-hunting kidnapper of John Fowles's 1963 novel, whose title describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowles titled his novel for its central figure, who gathers butterflies and finally a woman as specimens.

clue.text: Let down for Persephone?

definitions.meaning: a sense of being let down, a failure of hopes
Persephone was summoned to the underworld god Dis, so her fixed engagement there was a date with Dis

explanation.walkthrough: Dis is the Roman name for the god of the underworld; Persephone's compulsory stay with him is read whimsically as DIS + APPOINTMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Being let down, feeling dashed hopes, is a synonym; the second sense splits the word into Dis's meeting.

clue.text: De la Mare sadly loses a gem.

indicators.note: sadly signals the poet's name is scrambled, and loses says one letter is first removed from it

explanation.surface: The poet Walter de la Mare unhappily mislays a precious stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly loses' works on DE LA MARE: drop one A and rearrange the remaining DELMARE.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright green precious stone is a variety of beryl, a classic jewel.

clue.text: Mrs Masham who sounds and was great trouble-maker for the Duchess.

definitions.meaning: ... Masham, bedchamber woman and favourite of Queen Anne

definitions.text: who sounds and was great trouble-maker for the Duchess
definitions.meaning: spoken aloud the forename is 'a big ail', a great trouble, and she ousted Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough, from the Queen's favour

explanation.surface: Queen Anne's favourite was a great nuisance to the Duchess of Marlborough.
explanation.walkthrough: Abigail Masham supplanted Sarah, Duchess of Marlborough, as Queen Anne's favourite; her forename spoken aloud is 'a big ail', a great trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Masham, Queen Anne's bedchamber woman, was born with this forename, which also means a lady's maid.

clue.text: Woman of crosses, unlike 26, however.

parts.note: a woman of electoral rank, connected with the crosses marked on ballots by electors, rather than with memorial stone crosses

explanation.walkthrough: Electors mark crosses on ballot papers; the partner clue's woman is commemorated by the stone crosses of Edward I, so each is a woman of crosses in a different way.
explanation.definitionFit: The wife or widow of a German Elector, such as Sophia of Hanover, bore this title, linked here to voters' crosses.

clue.text: Conductor and a composition by poet.

parts.note: the indefinite article a takes the form an before a vowel
an ode is a lyric poem, a composition by a poet

explanation.surface: A musical conductor collaborates with a poet on a piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests an orchestra but means an electrical terminal.
explanation.definitionFit: The positive electrode through which current enters a device is an electrical terminal, a kind of conductor.

clue.text: Gather how Henry IV valued his city?

definitions.text: how Henry IV valued his city?
definitions.meaning: Henry IV of France reputedly said Paris was well worth a mass, so he priced it at that service

explanation.walkthrough: Henry IV converted to Catholicism to take Paris, reputedly saying 'Paris vaut bien une messe', Paris is well worth a mass.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather is to accumulate or heap up, a synonym; the second reading splits it into the price of Paris.

clue.text: Philipson's former wife gets in a heavy blow.

indicators.note: gets in means one piece enters and sits within another

parts.note: a lander is slang for a heavy punch that lands
an ex is a former spouse

explanation.surface: Philip's son's divorced spouse manages to land a hard punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Philipson' is a coinage for the son of Philip II of Macedon, the conqueror; 'gets in' is the container signal, and a lander is slang for a punch that connects.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip II of Macedon's son was the conqueror called the Great, so the clue's coinage names him by his father.

clue.text: Nothing stops him from praise: spoilt copy hasn't.

indicators.note: spoilt means damaged or messed up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A flatterer never stops praising, though his botched imitation lacks something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoilt' rearranges COPYHASNT; the apostrophe in hasn't gives no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawning flatterer heaps compliments on the powerful without pause, which is what the definition describes.

clue.text: Scene of Sam's Happy Valley, deep with certain protuberances.

parts.note: the deep is an abyss, a bottomless chasm
inia is the plural of inion, the bump at the back of the skull

explanation.surface: A setting where a happy valley lies deep among bumps and hills.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson's Rasselas opens in the Happy Valley, set in the old name for Ethiopia. INIA is the plural of inion, the bony bump at the back of the skull.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson set Prince Rasselas's secluded Happy Valley in the old African empire now called Ethiopia.

clue.text: Moore's charms of youth in conclusion, getting attention.

parts.note: the end is the conclusion
earing, an old form meaning lending an ear, is getting attention

explanation.surface: The poet's youthful charms, at the end, win notice.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Moore's song begins 'Believe me, if all those endearing young charms', so his charms of youth are described by this adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Moore's famous song calls youthful attractions lovable and winning, the adjective that pairs with them in its first line.

clue.text: This is not to imply no entry here is hopeless!

definitions.text: This is not to imply no entry here is hopeless!

parts.words: This is not to imply no entry here is hopeless
parts.note: split as '...' rather than 'imply no', and the place over whose gate Dante read 'Abandon hope, all ye who enter here'

explanation.walkthrough: Dante's hell bears the inscription 'Abandon all hope, ye who enter here'; the clue also plays on the classic confusion of imply with infer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante's first canticle names hell itself, a place of fire where entrants abandon all hope.

clue.text: Hangings arranged by Nebuchadnezzar, for a wonder.

definitions.text: Hangings arranged by Nebuchadnezzar, for a wonder.

parts.words: Hangings arranged by Nebuchadnezzar, for a wonder
parts.note: the Babylonian king is credited with the hanging terraced plantings, one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world

explanation.walkthrough: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, traditionally built by Nebuchadnezzar II, were one of the Seven Wonders of the World; 'Hangings' reads like drapery.
explanation.definitionFit: Babylon's famous terraced plantings, laid out as cultivated grounds, were reckoned among the ancient wonders.

clue.text: Abib preceded me ages ago; I arrive after two years.

indicators.note: after places the arrival piece behind the two years

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, so two of them make YY
AR is a timetable abbreviation for arrive or arrival

explanation.surface: A month speaks: an older month came before me, and I come along two years later.
explanation.walkthrough: Abib, later Nisan, is the first month of the Hebrew calendar, and this second month follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Hebrew calendar the spring month called Abib, later Nisan, is immediately followed by the second month, once called Ziv.

clue.text: Verdi's goodbye, also Tosti's.

parts.note: the Italian word of farewell sung in Violetta's aria in La Traviata and the title of a popular song by Paolo Tosti

explanation.walkthrough: Violetta sings 'Addio del passato' in Verdi's La Traviata, and Francesco Paolo Tosti wrote a famous song of farewell with this Italian title.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for farewell appears in Verdi's aria and as the title of Tosti's song.

clue.text: Author of French Mothers?

parts.note: du is French for of the
mas is an informal word for mothers

explanation.surface: Who wrote a book about French mothers?
explanation.walkthrough: 'French Mothers' looks like a book title, but 'of French' is DU, and MAS are mothers.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandre Dumas, father and son, were French novelists and dramatists, each an author.

clue.text: Sample of setter's deviousness.

indicators.note: a setter's deviousness is his trickery in reordering letters, so the words before it are scrambled

parts.note: the words of the clue as printed, which must be read as 'of a setter' to supply the nine letters that are rearranged

explanation.surface: A taste of the crossword compiler's cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, 'of setter's' gives only eight letters with no A; 'deviousness' rearranges OF A SETTER, so the setter evidently meant 'of a setter's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A foretaste is an advance sample, a small trial of what is to come.

clue.text: Blow from head of energetic old ox.

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the urus is the aurochs, an extinct wild ox

explanation.surface: A strike from the head of a vigorous ancient bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a strike, but it is a verb-turned-noun for the wind: this is the Greek east wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurus was the Greek god of the east wind, and a wind blows, so a blow stands for it.

clue.text: Sea-going explorer, one wrapped in wet blanket.

indicators.note: wrapped in means one piece is enclosed inside another

parts.note: a damper is a wet blanket, something that dulls enthusiasm
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A sailor-adventurer is bundled up in a soaking blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: William Dampier was the buccaneer-explorer who circumnavigated the globe three times.
explanation.definitionFit: William Dampier, the seventeenth-century English navigator, explored Australia's coast and sailed round the world three times.

clue.text: Woman of crosses, unlike 12,however.

parts.note: the queen of Edward I, whose funeral procession was marked by memorial stone crosses, rather than a woman linked to electors' ballot marks

explanation.walkthrough: Edward I raised twelve stone memorial crosses, such as Charing Cross, along his queen's funeral route; the partner clue's woman is linked to electors' crosses instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward I's queen, Eleanor of Castile, is commemorated by the twelve monuments that bear her name.

clue.text: Girl stood up and told to go by Waller.

definitions.meaning: a girl's name, from the flower
past tense of rise, got to one's feet
Edmund Waller's lyric begins 'Go, lovely' and names the flower it sends

explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Waller's poem opens 'Go, lovely Rose', so the flower is told to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A common girl's name, the past tense of getting up, and the flower addressed in Waller's lyric.

clue.text: Emerson advised improving to achieve celebrity with these plays.

definitions.text: Emerson advised improving to achieve celebrity with these plays.

parts.words: Emerson advised improving to achieve celebrity with these plays
parts.note: Emerson is credited with the saying that if you build a better trap for rodents the world will beat a path to your door; Hamlet's play and Agatha Christie's long-running play share that name

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'Build a better mousetrap and the world will beat a path to your door' is attributed to Emerson; Hamlet's play-within-a-play and Agatha Christie's record-running London play share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Spring traps for rodents are the devices of Emerson's saying, and the title of Hamlet's and Christie's plays.
